readerTitle: The beautiful design that was wrong
caseNote: 가상 사례 (수납함 제조사의 포장 디자이너, 일정 관리 앱의 제품 디자이너) · 적용 레슨: 기대치 설정 + 피드백 주기
insight: 전문가에게 일을 맡길 때는 '무엇과 왜'는 단단하게, '어떻게'는 느슨하게 정해 주고, 피드백은 해결책이 아니라 목표에 비춘 문제로 전한다.
misconception: 디자이너는 전문가이니 자유롭게 맡기고, 결과가 마음에 안 들면 '다시 해 보라'고 하면 된다.

sources.text: 이 유닛의 개념 레슨: 기대치 설정(PPL-02-05), 피드백 주기(PPL-02-03)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례와 수치(3미터 판독 거리, 2색 인쇄기, 사용자 테스트 5명 중 3명 이탈)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 연구나 통계로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
적용 레슨이므로 새 개념을 넣지 않았습니다. 기대치 설정과 피드백 주기 레슨의 용어·정의(예: 관찰한 행동과 그 영향을 말하는 피드백)와 표현이 일치하는지 게시 전에 맞춰 보세요.
다음 레슨 예고(Google이 관리자가 필요 없다는 것을 증명하려다 반대 결과를 얻었다는 Project Oxygen)는 PPL-02-09의 내용과 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The beautiful design that was wrong
body: Dana runs operations at a small company that makes plastic storage boxes. She hires its first designer, Leo, to redo the carton labels. "Make them look modern," she says. "You're the expert."
Three weeks later Leo shows a stunning design. Dana's stomach drops. It will never work on the packing line. Leo had no way of knowing why.

image.label: A sleek carton label next to a cluttered warehouse aisle
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 세련된 파스텔 톤 상자 라벨 시안이 모니터에 떠 있고, 오른쪽에는 상자가 높이 쌓인 창고 통로와 멀리서 지게차가 다가오는 모습. 두 장면 사이에 작은 물음표. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Rewind. How should Dana have briefed Leo?
body: Dana knows things Leo doesn't. The plant's printer does only two colors. Cartons sit stacked on racks, so people mostly see the short side. Forklift drivers read the size code from about 3 meters away.
What should her brief have looked like?

options.text: Keep it open: "modern, clean, your call". Experts do best with freedom
options.feedback: Freedom on the look is good. But without the goal and the limits, Leo has to guess, and a talented guess is still a guess. This is a gap in **setting expectations**.

options.text: State the goal, the hard limits and the deadline, and leave the look to Leo
options.feedback: This is **setting expectations**: be firm on what success means and what can't change, and loose on how to get there. Leo keeps the creative work and loses the guessing.

options.text: Send him three rival cartons and say "like these, but ours"
options.feedback: Examples show taste quickly. But they hide why things work, so Leo may copy the look and still miss the forklift and the printer.

cards.title: The limits lived only in Dana's head.
body: Leo's design used five colors, put the size code on the long side, and set it in a thin, elegant font. All good choices for a shop shelf. All wrong for a warehouse rack.
Dana knew the printer, the racks and the drivers. She had worked there for years and assumed those facts were obvious. Leo had worked there for three weeks.
A vague brief to a skilled person doesn't produce a bad design. It produces a **good answer to the wrong question**.

cards.title: Fix the what and why. Free the how.
body: Setting expectations means agreeing up front on what done looks like. With creative work, split the brief in two.
**Fixed:** the goal (drivers find the right box fast), the limits (two colors, readable at 3 meters, short side visible), the deadline, and how you'll judge it.
**Open:** layout, type, color, style. That's why you hired a designer.
cards.callout: Add an early check-in, such as rough sketches on day three, so a wrong turn costs days, not weeks.
cards.softwareNote: The same split works for any expert you manage, from an engineer to an accountant. Be clear on the problem and the limits, then let their skill decide the method.

cards.title: Draft two is close. Something feels off.
body: Leo's new label uses two colors and puts the code on the short side. Dana walks to the racks to test it. From the forklift seat, the size code is hard to read, and the green and gray look alike under the warehouse lights. She also just isn't keen on the font.
What does she tell Leo?

options.text: "It's not quite there. Can you try a few other directions?"
options.feedback: It's kind but gives Leo nothing to work with. He'll change things at random and may throw away what already works. Good **feedback** is specific.

options.text: "From 3 meters I couldn't read the code, and the two colors blur under our lights. The font is just my taste, so that's your call."
options.feedback: This is **giving feedback** well: describe what you saw and its effect on the goal, and keep personal taste separate from must-fix problems. Leo knows what to solve and still owns the design.

options.text: Mock up her own fix in a slide so Leo can see exactly what she means
options.feedback: Very clear, and fast this once. But it hands Leo a solution instead of a problem, and next time he'll wait for her slide.

cards.title: Name the problem, not the fix.
body: With experts, the most useful feedback describes the gap between the work and the goal. "I couldn't read it from the forklift" beats "make the font bigger." The designer may find a better fix than bigger type, such as more contrast or a bolder shape.
Also label each comment. Is it a **must** tied to the goal, or a **preference**? When everything sounds like a must, the designer stops using judgment and starts guessing what the boss likes.

image.label: Two speech bubbles: problem vs. prescribed fix
image.brief: 말풍선 두 개 비교. 왼쪽(초록 체크) "I couldn't read it from 3 m", 오른쪽(회색) "Make the font bigger". 왼쪽 말풍선 아래에서 여러 갈래 화살표가 다양한 해결책 아이콘으로 뻗어 나가고, 오른쪽은 화살표 하나만. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A brief can be too tight, or too sure.
body: Pile on limits and you've designed it yourself through a list. Keep the fixed part to what truly can't move.

Sometimes you don't know the goal yet. Maybe you're unsure whether the labels are even the real problem. Say so. Then the expectation becomes "explore three options and bring what you learn by Friday," not a finished design.
And feedback only helps if you've checked the work where it will be used: the rack, the phone screen, the real customer.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: You co-founded a scheduling app. Your product designer, Mia, is redesigning the sign-up flow. Your co-founder glances at her draft and says, "Make it pop." In a quick test, 3 of 5 new users quit at the screen asking for calendar access.
What do you tell Mia?

options.text: Pass on "make it pop" and trust her to work out what it means
options.feedback: It's a preference posing as a goal. Mia will polish the visuals while the real problem, users quitting, stays unsolved.

options.text: "Goal: more new users finish setup on day one. It must work on phones with no new backend. 3 of 5 testers quit at calendar access. Rough ideas Thursday?"
options.feedback: **Setting expectations** gives her the goal, the limits and a check-in. **Giving feedback** points at the observed problem. The how is still hers.

options.text: Let Mia run her own tests and decide everything, then review in a month
options.feedback: Lots of trust, and she may do great work. But with no shared goal or early check-in, a month is a long time to drift.

cards.title: Be firm on the goal, open on the craft.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Setting expectations:** agree on the goal, the hard limits, the deadline and an early check-in. **Giving feedback:** describe what you saw and its effect on the goal, and mark taste as taste.
**Try it today:** take one task you've handed to an expert. Write it down as two lists, "fixed" and "your call." Share it with them and ask what's missing.
